content: McArdle disease is a rare metabolic muscle disorder caused by the complete absence of the enzyme muscle glycogen phosphorylase. Individuals with this condition experience symptoms such as fatigue and muscle cramping within minutes of starting physical activity. They are also at risk of acute muscle damage, known as rhabdomyolysis, and acute kidney failure. However, if exercise is performed at a controlled pace during the initial few minutes, a phenomenon called the second wind can occur. This allows individuals to continue exercising, as their bodies begin to utilize alternative energy sources. Aerobic training has been shown to enhance exercise capacity by improving cardiovascular fitness. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of aerobic training on individuals with McArdle disease. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Neuromuscular Disease Group Specialized Register (as of January 11, 2011), CENTRAL (2010, Issue 4), MEDLINE (from January 1966 to January 2011), and EMBASE (from January 1980 to January 2011). The selection criteria included all randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials that investigated aerobic exercise training in individuals of any age diagnosed with McArdle disease. Two authors independently reviewed potential studies for inclusion and assessed their methodological quality. If more than one study of sufficient quality had been identified, a meta-analysis would have been conducted. Unfortunately, no randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials on aerobic training in individuals with McArdle disease were found. However, three open-label studies involving small numbers of participants provided some evidence that aerobic training can improve physical fitness in individuals with McArdle disease without causing adverse effects. The authors concluded that while the current evidence is limited to non-randomized studies with small sample sizes, these findings suggest that aerobic training is both safe and potentially beneficial for individuals with McArdle disease. Therefore, larger, well-designed controlled trials are warranted to further investigate the effects of aerobic training in this population.
